abstract: ABSTRACT Studies in animal models are essential to expanding the scope of interventions evaluated for safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy in clinical trials. Ferrets ( Mustela putorius furo ) are a key small-animal model for examining acquisition, replication, transmission, and disease manifestation, with particular relevance in modeling diverse viruses that target the respiratory tract. However, despite use in studies of vaccine immunogenicity and protection, as well as passive antibody transfer, there is little data characterizing antibody and Fc receptor biology in this species. To address this gap, ferret Fcγ receptors (FcγRI, FcγRII, FcγRIII) were identified and recombinantly expressed and characterized for binding to recombinant ferret and human IgG. In general, ferret IgG bound each receptor with slightly higher affinity than the human IgG subclasses, which exhibited similar ferret receptor binding profiles as observed for human receptors (IgG1 and IgG3 > IgG4 > IgG2). N-linked glycosylation motifs on ferret receptors were typically occupied, and binding was dependent on IgG Fc glycosylation. While further insight into the expression patterns and activities of innate immune cells stimulated by IgG is still needed, these data define Fc – FcγR recognition patterns in ferrets to help support optimal clinical translation of passive and active immunization studies.
methods:
Materials and methods
Construct design
The sequences of all Fc receptors were listed in Table S1, all of which included the human CD5 signal peptide (MPMGSLQPLATLYLLGMLVASCLG) on the N terminuses, and His6 tag followed by an AVI tag on the C terminuses, with linker GGG before and after His6 tag. The genes were codon optimized against human codons and synthesized (Genewiz), the inserts were cloned to the mammalian cell expression plasmid pCMV by HiFi assembly (NEBuilder® HiFi DNA Assembly). Ferret IgG expression plasmids were generously shared by the Kent and Wheatley labs as described.
60
A His6 tag was added to the C-terminus of the ferret IgG heavy chain. The sequences of ferret IgG heavy and light chains were listed in Table S2. The constructs of human monoclonal IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, and IgG4 were subclass switched variants of VRC01, a broadly neutralizing HIV-1 monoclonal Ab.
70
Human heavy and light chains were cloned in the pCMV plasmid but without any tag; detailed construct information can be found in the previous publication.
70
Recombinant protein expression and purification
Ferret Fc receptors, ferret IgG, and human monoclonal IgG subclasses were produced by transient transfection of Expi293F HEK cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using corresponding plasmids following the Expi293 Expression system user guide (Thermo Fisher Scientific). To express afucosylated human IgG1, the fucose analog 2-fluorofucose (2FF) (0.15 mM, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) was added to the culture approximately 4 hours post transfection. Ferret Fc receptors and IgG were first purified from culture supernatants by gravity columns using Ni NTA resin (Cytiva), and then the Fc receptors were further purified using a phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)-exchanged Superdex 75 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion chromatography column (Cytiva), while ferret IgG was further purified using Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion chromatography column (Cytiva), both on the ÄKTA pure FPLC system (Cytiva). Protein monomer was used for further analyses. The purified ferret Fc receptors were biotinylated for BLI analysis on the C terminal AVI tag using BirA biotin-protein ligase BirA500 kit (Avidity LLC.).
Human Fc receptors construction and expression were previously described.
72
Human monoclonal IgGs were first purified by gravity columns using protein A resin (Cytiva) in the case of IgG1, IgG2, and IgG4 or protein G (ThermoFisher) for IgG3, and then were further purified using a PBS-exchanged Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion chromatography column (Cytiva) on ÄKTA pure FPLC (Cytiva). Protein concentration was quantified by Braford Assay (Pierce).
Multi-alignment and phylogenetic analysis of Fc receptor sequences
Multiple sequence alignment of selected FcγR sequences was performed by Clustal Omega.
110
IQ-tree was used to build the phylogenetic tree by maximum likelihood with 1000 times of bootstrapping.
111
Geneious Prime was used to make the alignment figures and calculate the sequence identity. Ferret Fc receptor structures were generated using ColabFold v1.5.5: AlphaFold2 (“use_templates”: false, “relax_max_iterations”: 200, “num_recycles”: 3).
112
Structures were ranked by pLDDT with all top ranked structures yielding pLDDT scores >79. The predicted ferret Fc receptors and human Fc receptor overlay figures were generated in UCSF Chimera.
113
The contact residues between FcγR and IgG Fc were identified using buried solvent accessible surface area ≥15 Å
2
. RMSD values were calculated using UCSF Chimera.
Mass spectrometry sample preparation
Glycan occupancy rates were determined using a previously described method.
16
A 50 µg quantity of sample was denatured with 50 μL of 100% 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE) and 5 μL of 100 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at 55°C for 45 minutes. Samples were then alkylated by incubation with 3 μL of 550 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma) for 30 min at room temperature (RT) in the dark. Alkylation was quenched with 892 μL of 40 mM Tris-HCl, and protein was digested with either trypsin, GluC, or Chymotrypsin depending on the cleavage sites available. Trypsin digests occurred at a ratio of 1:30 (w/w) trypsin/protein for 16 hours at 37°C. GluC digests occurred at a ratio of 1:74 (w/w) GluC/protein for 12 hours at 25°C. Chymotrypsin digests occurred at a ratio of 1:74 (w/w) chymotrypsin/protein for 12 hours at 25°C. Formic acid was added to 1% (v/v) to quench the digestion, and the sample volume was reduced to ∼150 μL under vacuum. Peptides were then bound to a C-18 (Pierce, 89,870) column, washed three times with 0.1% formic acid, and eluted with a 60% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid solution. Eluate was concentrated under vacuum centrifugation and resuspended in 10 μL of 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate with heavy water (O18). Glycerol free PNGase (2,500 units, NEB, P0705) resuspended in heavy water (O18) was then added to the samples and incubated at 37°C for 1 hour. The reaction was then denatured at 100°C for 5 minutes and concentrated under vacuum centrifugation. Samples were resuspended in 0.1% formic acid and 5% acetonitrile in heavy water (H
2
18
O) at a final volume of 20 μL and frozen at −80°C until injection.
LC-MS/MS analysis
Samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry on an Easy-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid (Thermo Scientific). Peptides were first loaded onto an Acclaim PepMap 100 C18 trap column (Thermo Scientific) prior to separation on a 75 μm × 50 cm EASY-Spray C18 analytical column (Thermo Scientific) using a 1.6%–76% (v/v) acetonitrile gradient with 0.1% formic acid over 90 mins at 300 nL/min. Eluting peptides were injected directly into the mass spectrometer using an EASY-Spray source (Thermo Scientific). The instrument was operated in data-dependent mode with parent ion scans (MS1) collected at 120,000 resolution. Monoisotopic precursor selection and charge state screening were enabled. Ions with charge ≥ +2 were selected for collision-induced dissociation fragmentation spectrum acquisition (MS2) in the ion trap, with a maximum of 20 MS2 scans per MS1. Dynamic exclusion was active with a 15 s exclusion time after an ion is selected once. Each sample was run three times to generate technical replicate datasets.
Data analysis
Protein sequence databases were constructed by appending Fc receptor sequences to a database of background proteins comprising a consensus human protein database (Ensembl 73, longest sequence/gene) and a list of common protein contaminants (MaxQuant). Spectra were searched against the database using SEQUEST (Proteome Discoverer 2.4; Thermo Scientific). A precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm and fragment mass tolerance of 0.6 Da were used. The number of missed cleavages allowed varied depending on the protease used with Trypsin, GluC, and Chymotrypsin searches allowing for 2, 4, and 4 missed cleavages, respectively, as has been previously described.
114
Modifications of deaminated asparagine (H
2
18
O, and standard) and oxidized methionine (dynamic) were selected. Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were filtered using Fixed Value PSM Validator (Maximum Delta Cn = 0.05, Proteome Discoverer 2.4; Thermo Scientific). Peptide abundance was calculated from the extracted-ion chromatogram (XIC) peak area, as described.
72
For each peptide, a total XIC area was calculated as the sum of all unique peptide XIC areas of associated precursor ions. PSMs which yielded a ppm greater than 5 or were only detected once, were removed from the dataset. Similarly, PSMs that identified asparagine deamidations outside of putative glycosite were removed. Final glycan occupancy was determined by calculating the XIC ratio between peptides possessing deamidated and non-deamidated asparagine residues within the putative N-linked glycosylation site. Details regarding analysis of each receptor are presented in Table S3.
Multiplex array assay
Purified ferret, mouse and human Fc receptor proteins were coupled to carboxylated magnetic beads (Luminex) using amine reactive chemistry as previously described.
115
Ab samples were serially diluted, by 1:4, in 0.05% Tween-PBS in nonbinding, clear-bottom black 384-well plates (Corning) and one well of every dilution series contained no Ab was used as a background control. The master bead mix that contained all the receptor detection beads was prepared in 0.05% Tween-PBS with a concentration of 50,000 beads/ml for each bead set. The master bead mix was added to each well of Ab dilution plates and was sonicated for 10–20 s to mix and then placed on an XYZ plate shaker (IKA) at 1000 rpm for 2 h RT incubation for Fc receptor and Ab binding. Next, the unbound Abs were removed by washing the plate using an automatic plate washer (BioTek) fitted with a plate magnet programmed to conduct five washes with 60 ml of 0.05% Tween-PBS. Next, the secondary detection reagent for IgGs were prepared in 0.05% Tween-PBS, goat anti-ferret (IgGMA)-PE (Brookwood Biomedical, sab4004) was used to detect ferret IgG, goat F(ab’)2 anti-human IgG-PE (Southern Biotech, 1032–09) used to detect human IgGs and goat F(ab’)2 anti-mouse IgG(H+L)-PE (Southern Biotech, 2042–09) used to detect mouse IgGs, and added to each well. Plates were sonicated and then shaken at 1000 rpm at RT for 1 h. The plate was washed again, sheath fluid was used to resuspend beads in each well FlexMap 3D (Luminex) analysis. At least 35 beads for each bead set were analyzed. Data were exported, processed and visualized using Prism. To evaluate binding for each receptor-Ab pair, we calculated the average mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) and the corresponding standard deviations from the five samples at the lowest mAb concentrations (including blanks) and considered this value as the baseline. Binding was classified into four categories: high binding (average MFI of the top four concentrations > baseline MFI +100 SD), medium binding (signal between baseline MFI +100 SD and baseline +10 SD), low/no binding (signal less than baseline MFI +10 SD), and high background (baseline MFI > 1000).
Biolayer interferometry
Site-specifically biotinylated FcγR were loaded onto a streptavidin-coated biosensor (Sartorius) at 40 nM in BLI running buffer (1×PBS, pH7.4, with 0.02% Tween-20, 0.1% bovine serum albumin) for 60 s. The Abs were formulated at twice the intended concentration and diluted in BLI running buffer. The tested concentrations ranged from 1 µM for ferret IgG, human IgG1, and IgG3, 8.1 µM for human IgG2, and 0.833 µM for human IgG4, to approximately 1.4 nM for ferret IgG, human IgG1 and IgG3, 100 nM for human IgG2, and 3.4 nM for human IgG4, over a series of 1:3 dilutions. Association of the complex was measured over a 3 min period followed by 3 min of dissociation by Octet
Red
96 (ForteBio). The data were collected and analyzed by Octet Data Acquisition and Data Analysis HT, respectively. The plate containing the analytes was maintained at 30°C by the instrument over the course of the experiment.
Surface plasmon resonance
Abs of interest were prepared by covalent linkage to a carboxymethyldextran-functionalized biosensor (CMD200M, Xantec Bioanalytics) using a continuous flow microspotter (Carterra) capable of producing 96 discrete regions of interest. The microfluidic pathways were primed with 10 mM sodium acetate (pH 5.0) and activated for 5 minutes with 100 µL of 10.4 mM EDC and 1.4 mM sulfo-NHS (ThermoFisher) prepared in 10 mM MES (pH 5.0). Each Ab was prepared in 10 mM sodium acetate (pH 5.0) at concentrations ranging from 25 nM to 400 nM and along a 2-fold dilution series of at least two points. Ligand was flowed over the activated regions for 7 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of washing with sodium acetate. The sensor chip was loaded on a PBS +0.05% Tween 20-primed imaging-based SPR (MX96, IBIS Technologies) and quenched with a 150 µL injection of 1 M ethanolamine (pH 8.5). Fc receptors were formulated at 25 µM in PBS +0.05% Tween 20 and serially diluted over an 8-point 3-fold dilution series. The association time between IgGs and FcγRs was set at 300 s, and disassociation time at 400 s for ferret FcγRI and 300 s for ferret FcγRII(b) and FcγRIIIa. The instrument was maintained at 25°C throughout the experiment. Initial processing of the SPR data was performed using SprintX (IBIS Technologies). The signal from each region of interest on the sensor was referenced using the nearest unconjugated inter spot to account for bulk shifts and nonspecific binding. The blank injection immediately preceding each series of receptors was subtracted from the signal of each of the injections within a receptor series. Affinity values were further processed in Scrubber 2 (BioLogic Software) using k
on
and k
off
values for kinetic values and R
max
values of each analyte concentration at equilibrium for equilibrium fitting.

body:
Introduction
Viral infection and resulting disease are often studied in small animal models
1
to understand viral acquisition,
2
viral shedding,
3
,
4
disease progression,
5
as well as to test vaccines
3
,
6
and develop therapeutics.
7
,
8
Ferrets (
Mustela putorius furo
) are a standard small animal model for human infection by respiratory viruses
9
including influenza,
10
respiratory syncytial virus,
11
and SARS-CoV.
12
Ferrets are often a small animal model of choice as they share respiratory tract physiology to humans
13
that both recapitulates the severity of disease
10
and enables study of disease progression and treatment outcome.
14
Ferrets have long been used as a valuable model of influenza infection.
15
In comparison to other small animals such as mice or pigs, both ferret lung physiology and the distribution of the entry receptor for influenza, sialylated cell surface proteins, throughout the respiratory tract is closer to that of humans.
16
These similarities allow ferret infection by zoonotic
17
and human
18
strains of influenza without manipulation of the host animal, thereby serving as a faithful model of human influenza pathogenicity and transmission, as well as disease symptoms, progression across tissues, and outcomes.
18
Further, influenza studies in ferrets have been used to validate candidate vaccines,
19–23
therapeutic antibodies (Abs),
24
,
25
and to study influenza disease and treatment in vulnerable populations.
26
,
27
Among others, these studies have established ferret models as a key tool in human health advances.
28
During the COVID pandemic, the homology of human and ferret angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) enabled the use of ferrets as models of SARS-CoV-2 infection
5
without the genetic manipulation needed in mice. As for influenza and other coronaviruses,
29
,
30
infection of ferrets with SARS-CoV-2 leads to infection, mild symptomatic disease, and viral shedding.
5
Importantly, the titers of Abs raised in ferrets against SARS-CoV-2 infection and candidate vaccines have shaped our understanding of infection and helped advance vaccine and therapeutic Ab products through preclinical testing.
7
,
31–34
For many respiratory viruses, particularly influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the neutralizing humoral responses
35
,
36
and T cell responses
37
to infection and vaccination have been well studied in ferrets. On the other hand, little work has been done to evaluate the Fc effector, also called the non-neutralizing, humoral activity in response to infection or vaccination in ferrets. Within each species, the binding affinities of Abs to Fc receptors vary across Ab isotypes, subclasses, and glycosylation state, as well as by receptor type.
38–40
Additionally, the expression of Fc receptors varies across immune cells.
41
The binding of Ab to Fc receptors can be inhibitory
41
,
42
or may drive effector activities including antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP), and complement-dependent cytotoxicity.
43
In humans, Fc effector function of humoral responses has been associated with protection from infection from viruses including Ebola,
44
Malaria,
45
RSV,
46
and HIV,
47
among others. Further, differences in Fc effector activity,
48
Fc glycosylation,
49–51
and Fc receptor binding
49
are associated with differences in the severity of COVID disease in infected patients. While these examples highlight the importance of Fc effector function, this understanding can be difficult to translate from small animal model to the clinical setting as Ab subclasses, glycosylation patterns, Fc receptors, and expression patterns can all vary across species.
52–54
In addition to supporting translation, characterization of Fc effector function within small animal models such as mice
55
and nonhuman primates
56
has helped to identify protective aspects of the humoral response that might be leveraged in the design and optimization of vaccines and Ab therapeutics.
In ferrets, studies of the Fc effector function of both active and passive immunity have been historically hampered by both a lack of available reagents and an incomplete sequencing of ferret Abs and Fc receptors. Most studies that have characterized ferret immune responses have used commercially available Abs for human, mouse, or other animals that have cross-reactivity with ferret molecules.
28
,
57
Recently, purification of ferret Abs of different isotypes,
58
sequencing of the ferret genome
59
and targeted sequencing of ferret B cell receptors
60
,
61
have been completed. These efforts allow for identification of ferret Fc receptors and Ab types. Some of this recent work suggests that ferrets have the potential to serve as better models of Ab biology than mice. For example, though human IgG is reported to be less long-lived in ferrets than it is in humans,
62
the ferret neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) has greater (~80%) identity to human FcRn than does mouse FcRn (66% identity). Further, unlike in mouse models,
63
Abs with Fc domain modifications that extend plasma half-life in humans also extend half-life in ferrets.
64
Here, leveraging recent sequencing-based efforts, we characterize the molecular interactions between ferret and human IgG and ferret Fcγ receptors (FcγR) that underpin ferret humoral immune responses and provide a basis for comparison between human and ferret responses in studies of vaccines and therapeutic Abs in this important preclinical model.
Results
Identification and phylogenetic analysis of ferret Fcγ receptors
Human and mouse FcγR sequences (
Table S1
) were used to search for homology within the published ferret genome,
59
resulting in identification of putative ferret orthologs of FcγRI (
XP_004776893.2
), FcγRII (
XP_044942493.1
), and FcγRIIIa (
XP_004751441.2
). Ferret receptors exhibited similar putative domain architecture as human and murine receptors (
Figure 1(A)
), with FcγRI presenting three and FcγRII and RIII receptors presenting two extracellular domains. Whereas FcγRI and FcγRIII are presumed to interact with the common γ chain for signaling, ferret FcγRII contains an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif (ITIM) V/I/xYxxL/V (
Figure S1
), suggesting a role as an inhibitory receptor, and closest homology to the human FcγRIIb and murine FcγRIIb receptors in the intracellular regions; thus, ferret FcγRII is referred to as FcγRII(b) in this study. No ortholog of the human FcγRIIa or FcγRIIc receptors, which bear intracellular immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activating motif (ITAM) sequences, nor the murine FcγRIII receptor, which is most similar in sequence to FcγRII receptors in other species, despite their alternative numbering, were identified. Lastly, ferret FcγRIIIa was most similar to human FcγRIIIa and murine FcγRIV, which also lack intrinsic signaling motifs and are known to rely on the γ chain.
Figure 1.
Domain structure and sequence homology of ferret FcγRs. A. Schematic illustrating the domain architecture of Fc receptors in human (left), ferret (center), and mouse (right). Extracellular domains are indicated as D1, D2, and D3. Signaling motifs include immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (itam, green) and immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motifs (itim, red). The γ-chain serves as a common signaling component. B. Phylogenetic tree depicting the evolutionary relationships among full length FcγRs sequences in human, ferret, and other model animal genomes. Using the human numbering convention, FcγRI (magenta), FcγRII (RIII) (dark blue), and FcγRIII (riv) (brown) form distinct clades. Bootstrap support values are indicated at the nodes. C. Percent identity observed among FcγR in human, rhesus, mice, and ferrets.
Broader phylogenetic analysis of full-length ferret FcγRI, FcγRII (b), and FcγRIIIa with human, rhesus macaque, mouse, and other animals made clear the grouping of receptors across families (
Figure 1(B)
). As compared to mouse, the most frequently used small animal model, ferret FcγR exhibited a greater degree of identity to human FcγRI, similar identity to human FcγRII, and decreased sequence identity to human FcγRIII (
Figure 1(C)
).
Sequence alignment, structural modeling, and N-glycosylation analysis of ferret FcγRs
Sequence alignments across human, rhesus macaque, mouse, and ferret FcγRI extracellular domains demonstrate conservation (
Figure 2(A)
). Of the 15 predicted ferret FcγRI contact residues based on the human FcγRI:IgG co-crystal structure (PDB: 4w4o),
65
10 are identical to human FcγRI (
Figure 2(B)
). Despite sequence diversity, a model of ferret FcγRI superimposing the modeled ferret structure onto that observed for human showed a high degree of consistency on contact residue side chain positioning, with root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.727 (
Figure 2(C)
). Five predicted N-linked glycosylation motifs (NXS/T) were identified in ferret FcγRI extracellular region. While the human FcγRI extracellular region presents six, only two (N61 and N161 of ferret FcγRI) are conserved, both of which are outside of predicted contact regions. While N131 is within the predicted contact region, its side chain appears positioned away from the Fc interface. Though not all peptides were detected, analysis of site-specific N-glycan site occupancy by mass spectrometry demonstrated a high degree of occupancy (
Figure 2(D)
), consistent with diffuse bands observed in SDS-PAGE (
Figure S2
).
Figure 2.
Sequence and structure analysis of ferret FcγRI. A. Sequence alignment of ferret, human, mouse and rhesus macaque FcγRI extracellular domains. Human FcγRI extracellular domains are denoted in blue, human and ferret FcγRI N-linked glycosylation motif sites are denoted in purple, human IgG contact residues in cyan, while predicted ferret contact residues are in green. B. Structural model of domains 1 and 2 of human FcγRI (blue): human IgG Fc (gray) co-crystal structure based on PDB 4w4o. The side chains of amino acids that exhibit variation between human and ferret within (cyan) and outside (red) of the contact interface are illustrated on human FcγRI ribbon backbone. N-linked glycosylation motif sites are denoted in purple. C. Binding pocket of human FcγRI (blue) and IgG Fc (gray), predicted structure ferret FcγRI (green) is overlaid with human FcγRI, with root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.727. Side chains of predicted contact residues of ferret FcγRI are illustrated. D. N-glycan occupancy of ferret FcγRI asparagine residues in N-linked glycosylation motifs. N.D., not detectable.
Ferret FcγRII (b) falls in the same clade as human FcγRIIa, FcγRIIb, FcγRIIc, rhesus macaque FcγRIIa, FcγRIIb, and mouse FcγRIIb and FcγRIIIa (
Figure 1(B)
). It has higher identity with human FcγRIIb (55.4%) than with rhesus macaque FcγRIIb (50.7%) or mouse FcγRIIb (50.8%) (
Figure 1C
). Based on the co-crystal structure of human FcγRIIb with IgG (PDB: 3wjj),
66
six of nine predicted ferret FcγRII (b) contact residues are identical with human FcγRIIb, and there are numerous differences outside of the binding interface (
Figure 3(A,B)
). Nonetheless, the overall fold and binding region appears structurally well-conserved, the RMSD of ferret FcγRII (b) and human FcγRIIb is 0.727 (
Figure 3(C)
). The extracellular domain of ferret FcγRII (b) has four predicted N-linked glycosylation motifs, one of which (N187) is conserved, though distal to contact residues. All four N-glycan motifs were highly occupied (
Figure 3(D)
).
Figure 3.
Sequence and structure analysis of ferret FcγRII(b). A. Sequence alignment of ferret, human, mouse and rhesus macaque FcγRII extracellular domains. Human FcγRIIb extracellular domains are denoted in blue, human and ferret FcγRII(b) asparagine residues of N-linked glycosylation motifs are denoted in purple, and IgG contact residues for human FcγRIIb in cyan, and predicted ferret contact residues in green. B. Structural model of human FcγRIIb (blue): human IgG (gray) co-crystal structure based on PDB 3wjj. The side chains of amino acids that exhibit variation between human and ferret within (cyan) and outside (red) of the contact interface are illustrated on the human FcγRIIb ribbon backbone. C. Binding pocket of human FcγRIIb (blue) and IgG Fc (gray), predicted structure ferret FcγRII(b) (green) is overlaid with human FcγRIIb, with RMSD of 0.727. The side chains of predicted contact residues of ferret FcγRII(b) are illustrated. D. N-glycan occupancy of ferret FcγRII(b) asparagine residues in N-linked glycosylation motifs.
Ferret FcγRIIIa falls in the same clade as human FcγRIIIa, FcγRIIIb, rhesus macaque FcγRIII and mouse FcγRIV. Its identity is greater to rhesus macaque FcγRIII (58.2%) than human FcγRIII (~54%) or mouse FcγRIV (50.4%) (
Figure 1(C)
). Based on the human FcγRIIIa-IgG Fc co-crystal structure (PDB: 5xje),
67
only five of 16 predicted ferret FcγRIIIa contact residues are identical to human FcγRIIIa (
Figure 4(B)
). Amino acid substitutions within and outside the contact interface are numerous, the protein fold is modeled as less conserved, with an RMSD of 0.928 (
Figure 4(C)
). Like human FcγRIIIa, ferret FcγRIIIa has four predicted N-linked glycosylation motifs in its extracellular domain, ferret N63 and N179 are conserved (
Figure 4(A)
). Importantly, the presence of a glycan at human N162 (ferret N179) of this receptor is known to influence the preferential binding of afucosylated IgG Fc, and this motif is common across species.
68
N-glycan occupancy was high across all motifs in ferret FcγRIIIa and was complete at N179, the functionally important residue (
Figure 4(D)
).
Figure 4.
Sequence and structure analysis of ferret FcγRIIIa. A. Sequence alignment of ferret, human, mouse and rhesus macaque FcγRIII (murine iv) extracellular domains. Human FcγRIIIa extracellular domains are denoted in blue, human and ferret FcγRIIIa asparagine residues of N-linked glycosylation motifs are denoted in purple, human IgG contact residues in cyan, and predicted ferret contact residues in green. B. Structural model of human FcγRIIIa (blue): human IgG (gray) co-crystal structure based on PDB 5xje. The side chains of amino acids that exhibit variation between human and ferret within (cyan) and outside (red) of the contact interface are illustrated on the FcγRIIIa ribbon backbone. N-linked glycosylation sites are denoted in purple. C. Binding pocket of human FcγRIIIa (blue) and IgG Fc (gray), predicted structure ferret FcγRIIIa (green) is overlaid with human FcγRIIIa, with RMSD of 0.928. The side chains of predicted contact residues of ferret FcγRIIIa are illustrated. D. N-glycan occupancy of ferret FcγRIIIa asparagine residues in N-linked glycosylation motifs.
Sequence alignment and structural modeling of ferret IgG
To date, B cell sequencing from ferrets has identified only a single IgG subclass.
60
As defined by the human FcγRIIIa-IgG Fc co-crystal structure (PDB: 5xje), ferret differs from human IgG at three to five putative FcγR contact residues, though the exact predicted contact residues differ depending on the IgG subclass and receptor (
Figure 5(A)
). The N-linked glycosylation important to FcγR binding in other species (N297 in human IgG1) is conserved in ferrets. Numerous residues differ at other sites (
Figure 5(B)
), including CH2 and CH3 domains, to which the neonatal FcR receptor (FcRn) and other Ig binding proteins such as Protein A and protein G bind. A top down view of the IgG Fc shows a number of substitutions along the periphery of the FcγR binding interface (
Figure 5(C)
). At 68% identity, the ferret IgG sequence is most similar to IgG1 in humans and to IgG3 in mice (
Figure 5(D)
).
Figure 5.
Sequence and structural alignment of ferret IgG CH2 and CH3 domains. A. Sequence alignment of IgG CH2 and CH3 domains across species and subclasses. Human FcγRIIIa contact residues are annotated in cyan, the conserved N-glycosylation site is in purple. B. Structural model of human IgG1 CH2 and CH3 domains (ribbon) in complex with human FcγRIIIa extracellular domain (space-fill) (pdb 5xje). Amino acids that differ between ferret IgG and human IgG1 sequences are colored red and cyan, when outside or within the predicted contact interface, respectively. Oligosaccharides at N297 are illustrated in ball and stick. C. Top-down view of the FcγR binding pocket of human IgG. D. Percent identity observed among IgG CH2 and CH3 domains across species.
Cross-species binding interactions between Fc receptors and immunoglobulins
To support analysis of ferret FcγR and IgG, the extracellular domains of ferret FcγRI, FcγRII(b), and FcγRIIIa were recombinantly expressed with C terminal 6xHis and AVI tags and were purified using a two-step purification method by Ni-NTA and SEC columns (
Figure S2 and Table S2
). The sole ferret IgG subclass reported to date was recombinantly expressed with a lambda light chain
69
(
Table S2
), as were subclass switched forms of human IgG1, IgG2, IgG3 and IgG4 in the context of the same Fv and light chain.
70
,
71
A high throughput multiplex binding assay
72

Figure 6(A)
). Though the direct binding of some Ig detection reagents to some FcγR precluded collection of definitive data with all IgG-FcγR pairs and sensitivity to detect the lowest affinity interactions was lacking (
Figures S3 and S4
), this testing generally showed greater signal for both IgGs and FcγR expected to have higher affinity interactions. For example, FcγRI, known in mice and humans to present high affinity, exhibited binding at lower IgG concentrations than did FcγRII or FcγRIII. Ferret FcγRI exhibited the same trend both for IgGs from all three species (
Figure S3
), setting the expectation that it would likewise bind with high affinity. Similarly, among Abs, those subclasses in mice (IgG2a, IgG2c) and humans (IgG1, IgG3) known to exhibit better binding to FcγR showed these phenotypes with ferret FcγR as well (
Figure S4 and S5
). Ferret IgG showed FcγR binding similar to IgG subclasses in mice and humans with high receptor binding (e.g., human IgG1 and IgG3, mouse IgG2) (
Figure S3
).

Glycan dependence of IgG-FcγR binding in ferrets
To investigate the glycan-dependence of IgG-FcγR binding, recombinant ferret IgG and human IgG1 were treated with PNGaseF to remove N-linked glycans and screened in the multiplex assay. Removal of N-linked glycans from human IgG reduced binding to all ferret FcγR (
Figure 6B
). While binding to lower affinity receptors FcγRII (b) and FcγRIIIa was essentially undetectable, deglycosylation had a more modest effect on binding to ferret FcγRI. Similar results were observed for binding to these receptors when ferret IgG was deglycosylated (
Figure 6C
), although high background precluded meaningful analysis for ferret FcγRII(b).
Affinity characterization of ferret FcγR and IgG
To profile the recognition of ferret IgG and FcγR with greater resolution, a series of biolayer interferometry (BLI) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiments were conducted. For the former, each ferret FcγR was immobilized to the BLI tips through a C terminal biotin, mimicking the natural presentation of FcγR extracellular domains in cells. Binding affinities of monoclonal ferret IgG with ferret FcγRI, FcγRII (b), and FcγRIIIa were measured by BLI and compared with human IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, and IgG4 subclasses side by side (
Figure 7
). Ferret FcγRI showed the expected high-affinity binding profile for both ferret IgG and human IgG1, IgG3, and IgG4 but not IgG2, whose binding could not be quantified (
Figure 7(A)
). Ferret IgG exhibited a similar affinity as human IgG1 (K
D
3.7 nM and 2.9 nM, respectively), as well as the slow dissociation rate typical of this receptor in other species.

The limited resolution of this approach to quantify some interactions motivated further testing, including technical replicates using multiplexed SPR. For these experiments, the assay format was inverted: Abs of interest were covalently immobilized onto an SPR chip surface through conjugation via primary amines. An SPR chip containing Abs in discrete, replicated spots was simultaneously loaded with each ferret FcγR within the same SPR flow cell, providing for coincident evaluation of FcγR affinity for each IgG.
In this format, the slow-on, slow-off rate of ferret FcγRI and its high affinity, the intermediate rates of ferret FcγRIIIa, and the fast rates of FcγRII (b) for both ferret IgG (

) and human IgG were clear (
Figure S6-S8
). Excellent agreement was observed across replicates (

), and testing demonstrated highest affinity of ferret IgG for each of the ferret FcγR, followed closely by human IgG1 and IgG3, then IgG4. Human IgG2 bound only weakly, exhibiting one to four orders of magnitude poorer binding affinity than ferret IgG1. With this method, both equilibrium and kinetic K

D

Lastly, to investigate potential affinity differences in the binding of ferret FcγRIIIa to fucosylated versus afucosylated IgG, the fucose analog 2-fluorofucose was added during protein expression to limit fucose modification of human IgG1. The presumably afucosylated human IgG1 expressed in this way showed increased affinity to ferret FcγRIIIa by about three-fold (
Figure S9A, D
). While this effect was somewhat less pronounced than that observed for either 158F or 158 V allotypes of human FcγRIIIa (
Figure S9B-D
), this observation suggests that the enhanced activity of afucosylated IgG would be recapitulated in the ferret model.
Discussion
This work has characterized recombinant ferret FcγR and IgG through sequence alignments, affinity assays, and site-specific glycosylation analysis. Importantly, these results provide genetic, structural, and biophysical analysis of ferret Ab and FcγR features that underpin species-specific and cross-species Fc-FcγR interactions relevant to the use of this model in immunization and passive human Ab transfer studies. For the latter, the half-life of IgGs may vary in association with species-specific differences in IgG and FcRn.
In terms of Ab biology, ferret IgG showed high similarity with human IgG1 in binding all ferret FcγRs in affinity analyses, suggesting that Ab responses induced by candidate vaccines tested in this model will exhibit similar functions as the IgG1-biased responses typically observed to result from both natural infection
73–77
and vaccination
73
,
78–80
in humans. To the extent that human IgG2, IgG3, and IgG4 contribute to protection and pathology in the clinic, their unique effects will not be recapitulated in active immunization studies as orthologs of these subclasses are apparently not represented in ferrets. Effects of afucosylation in increasing the inflammatory potential of Abs via increased affinity to FcγRIII have the potential to also be present in ferrets, suggesting that afucosylated monoclonal Abs could be effectively tested. However, the ability of immunization or infection to drive increases in Ab Fc afucosylation in this model, as has been observed in humans,
50
,
81
is not yet established. Relevant to the former, development of monoclonal Abs for treatment of COVID-19 disease was often pursued with human IgG1 molecules mutated to eliminate their effector function
82
; data in this study suggest that the benefits or risks of maintaining effector function could be meaningfully tested in the ferret model. Though we did not test a panel of non-native Fc domain variants in this study, our data, in addition to prior studies of rhesus
83
,
84
and mouse
85
,
86
FcγR binding preferences, demonstrate that Abs of a given sequence tend to exhibit conserved activities across FcγR from different hosts.
Greater differences between the clinic and its models may be driven by distinctions in effector cell populations and their biology. While all major FcγR classes are represented in ferrets and their general affinity profiles mirrored those present in other species well, a narrower set of homologous receptors was observed. Humans express up to six distinct FcγR. The low-affinity FcγRIIIb expressed on human neutrophils,
87
which lacks a transmembrane domain and instead bears a glycophosphatidylinositol anchor, and FcγRIIc, which is expressed in only a subset of individuals and composed of the extracellular domain of FcγRIIb and intracellular domain of FcγRIIa,
88
,
89
appear to be unique to humans. Among the three FcγRII sequences present in humans, the ferret genome appears to encode only an ortholog to human FcγRIIb, the low affinity inhibitory receptor expressed more broadly than other human Fc receptors, present on lymphoid, myeloid, and granulocyte cells, including B cells, monocyte, macrophage, neutrophil, mast cell, and other immune cells.
90
In contrast, the ITAM-bearing human FcγRIIa plays important roles in driving phagocytosis and inflammation.
91
Its apparent absence from the ferret genome may have implications for use of this model. As mice lack an ortholog of human FcγRIIa, human FcγRIIa-transgenic mice have been developed and used to recapitulate and study disease in studies of thrombosis.
92
,
93
The expression of human FcγRIIa on platelets in this transgenic model is a key factor in IgG-dependent anaphylaxis, consistent with the observation that stronger platelet activation can be linked to more severe anaphylaxis in patients suffering from drug-induced anaphylaxis.
94
As ferrets lack an ortholog to human FcγRIIa, the drug-induced anaphylaxis triggered by human platelets might not be observed in ferrets. In addition to these toxicities, the benefits of Ab binding to human FcγRIIa on effector cells may not be captured well in the ferret model.
Nonetheless, ferret IgG showed very good binding with ferret FcγRI and FcγRIII(a), which signal through their own or accessory ITAMs, leading to effects such as activation of ADCP, ADCC, and inflammatory mediators and cytokines release in other species.
42
,
95
Ferret IgG also bound to ferret FcγRII(b), the ITIM-bearing inhibitory regulator of immune responses by modulating both B cell responses and effector cell functions, such as macrophage phagocytosis in human and mouse.
42
,
96
While single cell transcriptomic studies may offer the potential to define the putative immune cell types and their putative FcγR expression patterns, there are limited ferret-specific reagents available to characterize expression levels. The panel of recombinant FcγR established here offer the opportunity to screen reagents developed for other species for cross-reactivity in ferrets or to develop novel reagents that could enable further understanding of Fc and FcγR biology for Fc-mediated effects in diverse immune cells. Motivating such effort, ferrets generally show higher identity and similarity to humans than do mice from both genetic and anatomical perspectives, which may make them a superior animal model for studies on human respiratory diseases. Yet, as noted above, beyond their larger size, a considerable obstacle facing ferret testing in preclinical trials is the lack of immunological reagents, which hampers immune cell phenotyping and mechanistic insights.
Glycosylation of human FcγR plays important roles in regulating Fc receptor-mediated immunity, and further affect human health and may cause disease in cases of abnormal glycosylation modifications.
97
,
98
Decreased Ab binding levels and altered binding kinetics are observed for enzymatically deglycosylated human FcγRI and FcγRIII.
99
As noted above, glycosylation on human FcγRIIIa N162 is necessary for the high binding affinity to nonfucosylated IgG1, while the glycosylation on human FcγRIIIa N45 hindered the high binding affinity to afucosylated IgG1.
100
This trend might apply to ferret FcγRIIIa, as human FcγRIIIa N45 and N162 are both conserved in ferret FcγRIIIa. Human FcγR glycosylation varies among different cell types from isolated human cells or engineered human embryonic kidney (HEK) and Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells used for mammalian protein expression.
101–103
In this study, we used the Expi293F cell line for recombinant expression of ferret FcγRs and IgG and performed site-specific N-glycosylation analysis on these ferret FcγRs, which may well differ from the glycosylation in primary ferret cells.
There is only one conserved N-linked glycosylation site in the Fc region of human IgG1 (N297), IgG2, IgG4 and ferret IgG (N302), but two N-linked glycosylation sites in human IgG3 Fc.
104
Removing N-glycans from human IgG reduces or abolishes binding to human FcγRs.
105
,
106
Removal of N-glycans of ferret IgG and human IgG1 performed in this study also significantly reduced binding to ferret FcγRs. As a more subtle form of glycovariation, the absence of core fucose in human IgG can significantly increase affinity for human FcγRIIIa,
107
an effect that extends across a diversity of mammalian hosts.
108
Zou et al. analyzed the N-glycans in IgG purified from ferret and found that ferret IgGs are diverse and that, like human serum IgG, ferret IgG is typically core-fucosylated.
109
Afucosylated ferret IgG may also show higher affinity to ferret FcγRIIIa given conservation of glycosylation on a receptor site that drives this affinity difference, and its observation in the context of greater stimulation of reporter cell lines expressing ferret FcγRIIIa by afucosylated human IgG,
108
consistent with our
in vitro
observation that afucosylated human IgG has higher affinity to ferret FcγRIIIa than fucosylated human IgG1. Meanwhile, both modification with galactose and high-mannose can increase binding to human FcγRIIIa and lead to high ADCC responses in human IgG.
104
Understanding if the “fucose effect” and effector cell biology are comparable between ferrets and humans in the context of native ferret effector cells has the potential to motivate use of this model to interpret the mechanistic importance of the increased afucosylation of SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG observed in severe COVID-19 disease.
50
,
81
Overall, this work provides support to the suitability of studies of human IgG Abs in protecting against various viruses in the ferret animal model from a molecular perspective. Though further cellular profiling will be critical to better understanding of the aspects on Ab and FcγR biology that may be conserved or distinct between species, data here aid in interpretation of preclinical studies using the ferret model in providing insight into the comparability of humoral immune responses and their functions, guiding Ab engineering, efficacy evaluation, and safety testing for future therapeutic applications and basic pathogenesis studies.
Materials and methods
Construct design
The sequences of all Fc receptors were listed in Table S1, all of which included the human CD5 signal peptide (MPMGSLQPLATLYLLGMLVASCLG) on the N terminuses, and His6 tag followed by an AVI tag on the C terminuses, with linker GGG before and after His6 tag. The genes were codon optimized against human codons and synthesized (Genewiz), the inserts were cloned to the mammalian cell expression plasmid pCMV by HiFi assembly (NEBuilder® HiFi DNA Assembly). Ferret IgG expression plasmids were generously shared by the Kent and Wheatley labs as described.
60
A His6 tag was added to the C-terminus of the ferret IgG heavy chain. The sequences of ferret IgG heavy and light chains were listed in Table S2. The constructs of human monoclonal IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, and IgG4 were subclass switched variants of VRC01, a broadly neutralizing HIV-1 monoclonal Ab.
70
Human heavy and light chains were cloned in the pCMV plasmid but without any tag; detailed construct information can be found in the previous publication.
70
Recombinant protein expression and purification
Ferret Fc receptors, ferret IgG, and human monoclonal IgG subclasses were produced by transient transfection of Expi293F HEK cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using corresponding plasmids following the Expi293 Expression system user guide (Thermo Fisher Scientific). To express afucosylated human IgG1, the fucose analog 2-fluorofucose (2FF) (0.15 mM, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) was added to the culture approximately 4 hours post transfection. Ferret Fc receptors and IgG were first purified from culture supernatants by gravity columns using Ni NTA resin (Cytiva), and then the Fc receptors were further purified using a phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)-exchanged Superdex 75 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion chromatography column (Cytiva), while ferret IgG was further purified using Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion chromatography column (Cytiva), both on the ÄKTA pure FPLC system (Cytiva). Protein monomer was used for further analyses. The purified ferret Fc receptors were biotinylated for BLI analysis on the C terminal AVI tag using BirA biotin-protein ligase BirA500 kit (Avidity LLC.).
Human Fc receptors construction and expression were previously described.
72
Human monoclonal IgGs were first purified by gravity columns using protein A resin (Cytiva) in the case of IgG1, IgG2, and IgG4 or protein G (ThermoFisher) for IgG3, and then were further purified using a PBS-exchanged Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL size exclusion chromatography column (Cytiva) on ÄKTA pure FPLC (Cytiva). Protein concentration was quantified by Braford Assay (Pierce).
Multi-alignment and phylogenetic analysis of Fc receptor sequences
Multiple sequence alignment of selected FcγR sequences was performed by Clustal Omega.
110
IQ-tree was used to build the phylogenetic tree by maximum likelihood with 1000 times of bootstrapping.
111
Geneious Prime was used to make the alignment figures and calculate the sequence identity. Ferret Fc receptor structures were generated using ColabFold v1.5.5: AlphaFold2 (“use_templates”: false, “relax_max_iterations”: 200, “num_recycles”: 3).
112
Structures were ranked by pLDDT with all top ranked structures yielding pLDDT scores >79. The predicted ferret Fc receptors and human Fc receptor overlay figures were generated in UCSF Chimera.
113
The contact residues between FcγR and IgG Fc were identified using buried solvent accessible surface area ≥15 Å
2
. RMSD values were calculated using UCSF Chimera.
Mass spectrometry sample preparation
Glycan occupancy rates were determined using a previously described method.
16
A 50 µg quantity of sample was denatured with 50 μL of 100% 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE) and 5 μL of 100 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at 55°C for 45 minutes. Samples were then alkylated by incubation with 3 μL of 550 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma) for 30 min at room temperature (RT) in the dark. Alkylation was quenched with 892 μL of 40 mM Tris-HCl, and protein was digested with either trypsin, GluC, or Chymotrypsin depending on the cleavage sites available. Trypsin digests occurred at a ratio of 1:30 (w/w) trypsin/protein for 16 hours at 37°C. GluC digests occurred at a ratio of 1:74 (w/w) GluC/protein for 12 hours at 25°C. Chymotrypsin digests occurred at a ratio of 1:74 (w/w) chymotrypsin/protein for 12 hours at 25°C. Formic acid was added to 1% (v/v) to quench the digestion, and the sample volume was reduced to ∼150 μL under vacuum. Peptides were then bound to a C-18 (Pierce, 89,870) column, washed three times with 0.1% formic acid, and eluted with a 60% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid solution. Eluate was concentrated under vacuum centrifugation and resuspended in 10 μL of 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate with heavy water (O18). Glycerol free PNGase (2,500 units, NEB, P0705) resuspended in heavy water (O18) was then added to the samples and incubated at 37°C for 1 hour. The reaction was then denatured at 100°C for 5 minutes and concentrated under vacuum centrifugation. Samples were resuspended in 0.1% formic acid and 5% acetonitrile in heavy water (H
2
18
O) at a final volume of 20 μL and frozen at −80°C until injection.
LC-MS/MS analysis
Samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry on an Easy-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid (Thermo Scientific). Peptides were first loaded onto an Acclaim PepMap 100 C18 trap column (Thermo Scientific) prior to separation on a 75 μm × 50 cm EASY-Spray C18 analytical column (Thermo Scientific) using a 1.6%–76% (v/v) acetonitrile gradient with 0.1% formic acid over 90 mins at 300 nL/min. Eluting peptides were injected directly into the mass spectrometer using an EASY-Spray source (Thermo Scientific). The instrument was operated in data-dependent mode with parent ion scans (MS1) collected at 120,000 resolution. Monoisotopic precursor selection and charge state screening were enabled. Ions with charge ≥ +2 were selected for collision-induced dissociation fragmentation spectrum acquisition (MS2) in the ion trap, with a maximum of 20 MS2 scans per MS1. Dynamic exclusion was active with a 15 s exclusion time after an ion is selected once. Each sample was run three times to generate technical replicate datasets.
Data analysis
Protein sequence databases were constructed by appending Fc receptor sequences to a database of background proteins comprising a consensus human protein database (Ensembl 73, longest sequence/gene) and a list of common protein contaminants (MaxQuant). Spectra were searched against the database using SEQUEST (Proteome Discoverer 2.4; Thermo Scientific). A precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm and fragment mass tolerance of 0.6 Da were used. The number of missed cleavages allowed varied depending on the protease used with Trypsin, GluC, and Chymotrypsin searches allowing for 2, 4, and 4 missed cleavages, respectively, as has been previously described.
114
Modifications of deaminated asparagine (H
2
18
O, and standard) and oxidized methionine (dynamic) were selected. Peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were filtered using Fixed Value PSM Validator (Maximum Delta Cn = 0.05, Proteome Discoverer 2.4; Thermo Scientific). Peptide abundance was calculated from the extracted-ion chromatogram (XIC) peak area, as described.
72
For each peptide, a total XIC area was calculated as the sum of all unique peptide XIC areas of associated precursor ions. PSMs which yielded a ppm greater than 5 or were only detected once, were removed from the dataset. Similarly, PSMs that identified asparagine deamidations outside of putative glycosite were removed. Final glycan occupancy was determined by calculating the XIC ratio between peptides possessing deamidated and non-deamidated asparagine residues within the putative N-linked glycosylation site. Details regarding analysis of each receptor are presented in Table S3.
Multiplex array assay
Purified ferret, mouse and human Fc receptor proteins were coupled to carboxylated magnetic beads (Luminex) using amine reactive chemistry as previously described.
115
Ab samples were serially diluted, by 1:4, in 0.05% Tween-PBS in nonbinding, clear-bottom black 384-well plates (Corning) and one well of every dilution series contained no Ab was used as a background control. The master bead mix that contained all the receptor detection beads was prepared in 0.05% Tween-PBS with a concentration of 50,000 beads/ml for each bead set. The master bead mix was added to each well of Ab dilution plates and was sonicated for 10–20 s to mix and then placed on an XYZ plate shaker (IKA) at 1000 rpm for 2 h RT incubation for Fc receptor and Ab binding. Next, the unbound Abs were removed by washing the plate using an automatic plate washer (BioTek) fitted with a plate magnet programmed to conduct five washes with 60 ml of 0.05% Tween-PBS. Next, the secondary detection reagent for IgGs were prepared in 0.05% Tween-PBS, goat anti-ferret (IgGMA)-PE (Brookwood Biomedical, sab4004) was used to detect ferret IgG, goat F(ab’)2 anti-human IgG-PE (Southern Biotech, 1032–09) used to detect human IgGs and goat F(ab’)2 anti-mouse IgG(H+L)-PE (Southern Biotech, 2042–09) used to detect mouse IgGs, and added to each well. Plates were sonicated and then shaken at 1000 rpm at RT for 1 h. The plate was washed again, sheath fluid was used to resuspend beads in each well FlexMap 3D (Luminex) analysis. At least 35 beads for each bead set were analyzed. Data were exported, processed and visualized using Prism. To evaluate binding for each receptor-Ab pair, we calculated the average mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) and the corresponding standard deviations from the five samples at the lowest mAb concentrations (including blanks) and considered this value as the baseline. Binding was classified into four categories: high binding (average MFI of the top four concentrations > baseline MFI +100 SD), medium binding (signal between baseline MFI +100 SD and baseline +10 SD), low/no binding (signal less than baseline MFI +10 SD), and high background (baseline MFI > 1000).
Biolayer interferometry
Site-specifically biotinylated FcγR were loaded onto a streptavidin-coated biosensor (Sartorius) at 40 nM in BLI running buffer (1×PBS, pH7.4, with 0.02% Tween-20, 0.1% bovine serum albumin) for 60 s. The Abs were formulated at twice the intended concentration and diluted in BLI running buffer. The tested concentrations ranged from 1 µM for ferret IgG, human IgG1, and IgG3, 8.1 µM for human IgG2, and 0.833 µM for human IgG4, to approximately 1.4 nM for ferret IgG, human IgG1 and IgG3, 100 nM for human IgG2, and 3.4 nM for human IgG4, over a series of 1:3 dilutions. Association of the complex was measured over a 3 min period followed by 3 min of dissociation by Octet
Red
96 (ForteBio). The data were collected and analyzed by Octet Data Acquisition and Data Analysis HT, respectively. The plate containing the analytes was maintained at 30°C by the instrument over the course of the experiment.
Surface plasmon resonance
Abs of interest were prepared by covalent linkage to a carboxymethyldextran-functionalized biosensor (CMD200M, Xantec Bioanalytics) using a continuous flow microspotter (Carterra) capable of producing 96 discrete regions of interest. The microfluidic pathways were primed with 10 mM sodium acetate (pH 5.0) and activated for 5 minutes with 100 µL of 10.4 mM EDC and 1.4 mM sulfo-NHS (ThermoFisher) prepared in 10 mM MES (pH 5.0). Each Ab was prepared in 10 mM sodium acetate (pH 5.0) at concentrations ranging from 25 nM to 400 nM and along a 2-fold dilution series of at least two points. Ligand was flowed over the activated regions for 7 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of washing with sodium acetate. The sensor chip was loaded on a PBS +0.05% Tween 20-primed imaging-based SPR (MX96, IBIS Technologies) and quenched with a 150 µL injection of 1 M ethanolamine (pH 8.5). Fc receptors were formulated at 25 µM in PBS +0.05% Tween 20 and serially diluted over an 8-point 3-fold dilution series. The association time between IgGs and FcγRs was set at 300 s, and disassociation time at 400 s for ferret FcγRI and 300 s for ferret FcγRII(b) and FcγRIIIa. The instrument was maintained at 25°C throughout the experiment. Initial processing of the SPR data was performed using SprintX (IBIS Technologies). The signal from each region of interest on the sensor was referenced using the nearest unconjugated inter spot to account for bulk shifts and nonspecific binding. The blank injection immediately preceding each series of receptors was subtracted from the signal of each of the injections within a receptor series. Affinity values were further processed in Scrubber 2 (BioLogic Software) using k
on
and k
off
values for kinetic values and R
max
values of each analyte concentration at equilibrium for equilibrium fitting.
